question: Which part of the newborn's brain controls basic, automatic movements like primitive reflexes?
explanation: Primitive reflexes are managed by lower, subcortical areas of the brain before the higher cortical areas fully develop. [learn more](BMP214_U1_T5#BMP214_U1_T5_h1)

question: Why do primitive reflexes naturally fade as a baby gets older?

options.A: The baby's muscles become too heavy to move
options.B: The cerebral cortex matures and inhibits them
options.C: Frequent handling desensitizes the skin receptors
options.D: Nutritional deficiencies weaken the reflex arc

explanation: As the brain grows and matures, higher brain functions take over and naturally quiet down these automatic responses. [learn more](BMP214_U1_T5#BMP214_U1_T5_h1)

question: Which cranial nerve carries the touch signals that trigger a baby's rooting reflex?
explanation: The trigeminal nerve supplies feeling to the face, picking up the touch on the cheek or lip during rooting. [learn more](BMP214_U1_T5#BMP214_U1_T5_h2)

question: What is the main survival reason newborns have the rooting reflex?

options.A: Finding food and securing a breastfeeding latch
options.B: Strengthening the muscles of the neck and spine
options.C: Clearing mucus from the upper airway passages
options.D: Protecting the eyes from sudden bright lights

explanation: Turning toward a touch near the mouth helps the newborn find the breast or bottle for feeding easily. [learn more](BMP214_U1_T5#BMP214_U1_T5_h2)

question: How does a full-term newborn usually react when you gently stroke their upper lip?

options.A: Turns the head sharply toward the opposite shoulder
options.B: Tilts the head backward and opens the mouth
options.C: Extends both arms upward in a startle motion
options.D: Sucks vigorously on the examiner's bare finger

explanation: Stroking the upper lip prompts the baby to tilt back slightly and open the mouth to take in the nipple. [learn more](BMP214_U1_T5#BMP214_U1_T5_h3)

question: Why might a healthy newborn show a weak rooting reflex right after a big feed?

options.A: The infant is full and lacks motivation to feed
options.B: Excess body fat dampening facial skin sensors
options.C: Digestion temporarily blocks the trigeminal nerve
options.D: The baby is experiencing normal physiological shock

explanation: Babies who have just finished feeding are full, so their hunger drive is temporarily satisfied and they may ignore feeding cues. [learn more](BMP214_U1_T5#BMP214_U1_T5_h3)

question: Around what age does the rooting reflex normally disappear in a healthy infant?
explanation: As the higher brain centers mature over the first few months of life, the rooting reflex naturally fades away. [learn more](BMP214_U1_T5#BMP214_U1_T5_h4)

question: What does an equal and active rooting response on both sides of the face tell the midwife?

options.A: The baby is definitely ready to be introduced to solid foods
options.B: The mother had an entirely uncomplicated pregnancy and birth
options.C: The lower motor pathways and brainstem are functioning normally
options.D: The infant has received all necessary routine childhood immunizations

explanation: Equal responses on both sides show that the relevant brainstem structures and nerve pathways are working well. [learn more](BMP214_U1_T5#BMP214_U1_T5_h4)

question: What might an uneven (asymmetrical) rooting reflex suggest in a newborn delivered with vacuum assistance?
explanation: An uneven reflex on one side of the face often points to mild, temporary nerve trauma from an instrumental delivery. [learn more](BMP214_U1_T5#BMP214_U1_T5_h5)

question: Which of these conditions would most likely cause an absent rooting reflex across both sides of the face?

options.A: Severe birth asphyxia and central nervous depression
options.B: Mild physiologic jaundice fading on the third day
options.C: Normal mild weight loss in the first 48 hours
options.D: Transient skin rashes like erythema toxicum

explanation: When the central nervous system is depressed due to a lack of oxygen, automatic responses like rooting are weakened or temporarily lost. [learn more](BMP214_U1_T5#BMP214_U1_T5_h5)

question: When is the best time to use the rooting reflex to help start breastfeeding successfully?

options.A: During the golden hour immediately following birth
options.B: When the baby cries continuously for two hours
options.C: Just before the infant is discharged home from the ward
options.D: After the infant has received a full routine bath

explanation: Right after birth, during the golden hour, babies are naturally alert and ready to respond to feeding cues. [learn more](BMP214_U1_T5#BMP214_U1_T5_h6)

question: A mother shares that her newborn cries frantically and refuses to latch. What advice should you give based on rooting behavior?

options.A: Stop breastfeeding entirely and switch straight to artificial formula
options.B: Wait until the baby is completely exhausted so it will sleep at the breast
options.C: Look for early rooting cues like head turning before the baby starts crying
options.D: Force the baby's mouth open immediately regardless of head movement

explanation: Spotting early feeding cues keeps the baby calm and prevents them from getting overtired, making it much easier to latch. [learn more](BMP214_U1_T5#BMP214_U1_T5_h6)
